svg.aria-label: Diagram: CloudWatch alarms that use Prometheus Query Language can now trigger Amazon EC2 and Application Auto Scaling step and simple scaling policies, with two constraints stated in the announcement. Target tracking is not currently a supported policy type for PromQL alarms, and the query must return a single series and compare it to a threshold. The single-series requirement cuts across what a PromQL alarm normally does, because it selects metrics ingested through the CloudWatch OTLP endpoint, treats all matching time series as breaching, and tracks each breaching series independently as a contributor, entering ALARM when at least one contributor has breached longer than the pending period and returning to OK only when all contributors have recovered. So a scaling query is a different artefact from an alerting query: one wants labels, the other wants a scalar. Timing is duration-based rather than datapoint-based, using PendingPeriod which is equivalent to the Prometheus alert rule for duration, RecoveryPeriod which is equivalent to keep_firing_for, and EvaluationInterval for how often the query runs, which means a fleet with both PromQL and metric alarms has two models for how long before this reacts. The deeper change is ownership of the alarm. Under target tracking, Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling creates and manages the CloudWatch alarms and the documentation instructs you not to create, edit or delete them, and if the metric is missing data points the alarm goes to INSUFFICIENT_DATA and EC2 Auto Scaling cannot scale the group until new data points are found, which you cannot configure around because the alarm is not yours. Bringing your own PromQL alarm transfers that decision to you, and the CloudWatch default treatment is missing, which reproduces the same freeze without saying so. Auto Scaling actions also behave unlike notifications: an alarm invokes actions only on state change, except Auto Scaling actions which repeat once per minute while the alarm remains in the new state, which is sixty invocations in an hour. The unchanged hazard is that CloudWatch does not validate that the actions specified on an alarm exist, nor detect errors invoking nonexistent ones, so an alarm pointing at a deleted scaling policy transitions correctly and does nothing. Availability is scoped to all AWS Regions where CloudWatch PromQL alarms are available, and standard CloudWatch alarm pricing applies.
svg.title: PromQL can scale you, in exchange for the contributor model
svg.text: PromQL alarms can scale now. Two scopes, and a transfer of ownership.
“Target tracking is not currently a supported policy type for PromQL alarms.”
The single-series requirement switches off what PromQL alarms do differently
normally every matching series is a “contributor”, tracked independently
for scaling “The query must return a single series and compare it to a threshold”
Necessary — a step policy needs one number to measure distance past a threshold. But a scaling query is then
a different artefact from an alerting query: one wants labels, the other wants a scalar.
Duration-based, not datapoint counting
PendingPeriod = Prometheus “for”
RecoveryPeriod = “keep_firing_for”
Two timing models on one Auto Scaling group.
Actions repeat, unlike notifications
“once per minute that the alarm remains in the
new state” — 60 invocations in an hour.
Correct for scaling; different from an SNS alarm.
The real change: whose alarm it is
Target tracking. “Do not create, edit, or delete the CloudWatch alarms … EC2 Auto Scaling creates and
manages” them. And: “If the metric is missing data points … Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling cannot scale your
group until new data points are found.” A telemetry outage freezes scaling, unconfigurably.
Your own PromQL alarm. That decision becomes yours — and the CloudWatch default is
missing, which reproduces the same freeze without telling you it chose.
The hazard this release widens
Nothing validates the action exists. An alarm pointing at a deleted scaling policy transitions correctly and
does nothing — previously that lost a notification; now it can silently disable a capacity response.
Choose the missing-data treatment, and record why. Target tracking never let you.
Freezing capacity during a telemetry outage is often the safer answer. Treating it as breaching scales out on no
evidence. Neither is universally right, and leaving the default is choosing the first without noticing.
Scoped to “all AWS Regions where CloudWatch PromQL alarms are available” — a nested scope, not a global one.
If target tracking is working, nothing here is a reason to leave it.
